A bogus identi ty card in the name name of Shri Suraj Singh, cleaner T. No. 210 K Beggi Tunnelling Div i sion for the purpose of withdrawing the pay of Ashok kuma r. The appellants and the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff instituted a suit No. 157 of 1968 for a declaration and injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do in Predio ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28, 1974 on the ground that the plaintiff was not in possession of the suit property and, therefore, a suit for declaration simpliciter could not lie. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the suit was barred by res judicata as held by this Court in Dhondi Tukaram vs Hari Dadu AIR 1954 Bom 100; that the claim based on the factum of tenancy was not based on such allegation; and that the lease had terminated by efflux of time and defendant No 2 was, therefore entitled to let out the property to one of the defendants. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The decision rendered by the Civil Court would be without jurisdiction and, accordingly, it is directed that the issue whether defendant No1 was a tenant or a deemed tenant was required to be decided by Mamlatdar and the jurisdiction of the Civil court stood ousted by Section 58(2) of the Act. [1024B] 2. A mere declaration of his status as a tenant could not be granted unless the consequential relief for possession was prayed. The suit was filed on the basis that defendant No 1 was a trespasser and the plaintiff who had been dispossessed, by an act of trespass, lost his rights in the property. [ 1026C D] 3. So long as the subject matter of the second suit was directly and substantially in issue in the previous suit, the relief for land could not he gone into by the civil Court in view of the clear language of Section 7 read with Section 58 (2) specifically bars the jurisdiction to all other courts to settle, decide or deal with any question which is required to he settled, decided or dealt with by the Mamlatdar. [1009G] 4. The jurisdiction of Civil Court is specifically barred by sub section (2), of Section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any dispute which is by or under the Act required to been settled, decide and dealt with in accordance with the Mamlatdar 's recommendation. There can, therefore be no doubt that after the Fifth Amendment came into force the plaintiff had not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of land within the period allowed by Section 18 of the Tenancy Act, and had, therefore in order to get back his possession he was entitled to recover immediate possession of it on the strength of his tenancy.

The petitioners are engaged as carpenters 1st and 2nd grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the ' Corpo ration). They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution they are seeking enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay for equal work". Their claim is resisted by the respondents contending that the petitioners are doing the same duties and performing similar functions as that of "Senior Speech Therapist", "Audiologist" and "Speech Pathologist". Allowing the petition and dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: (1) It is not just a comparison of physical activity. [669C] Randhir Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to. (2) In service merit or experience could be the proper basis for classification to promote efficiency in administration and he or she learns also by experience as much as by other means. [668B C] (3) The discrimination complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management. A comparison cannot be made with counterparts in other establishments with different management, or even in establishments in different geographical location though owned by a same master. Unless it is shown that there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the life in the same establishment, the principle of "equal Pay for equal Work" cannot be enforced. [ 667B C D] (4) In the instant case the petitioners were employed by a Company incorporated under the and they can not claim wages payable to their counterparts situated in Government service. They cannot enforce the right to equal pay for Equal pay for equally work. The discrimination alleged against must be beyond the same liabi fide value owned by them. A distinction cannot be ex tended with counter affidavit in other establishment with different Management, or Even in establishments where there is no such distinction amongst the identical set Of employees by any one master in the Same establishment, that the principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitu tion which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. The discriminatory discrimination complained was only within the domain of Articles 14 and 16 which provides for equal pay in a particular cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. [667F G] (5) It would be irrational to suggest that equal pay should be payable for equal appoint ment to avoid stagnation or resultant frustration for lack of promotional avenues may also be allowed. A reference cannot be mad ed to the decision in Federation of All India Customs and Central Excise Stenographers (Recognition) vs Unionof India, AIR 1962 SC 1688, followed.

In the case it was alleged that in pursuance of the conspiracy and in furtherance of their common intention they committed the murder of A.1 on or about 10 November 1975, while according to the prosecution witnesses they were not the real culprits and had fabricated the deed of assignment put forward by the accused 1 to the deceased S.I. It was found by the Serologist that there is sufficient evidence against accused 6 in respect of charge No. 4 framed regarding the murder committed on the basis of which, no appeal against acquittal had been filed in the High Court and also the fact that accused 5 was not a party to charge No,4 which was framed only against accused 2, 3, 4 and 7, not against accused 1 and 6, in so far as it related to accused 2 no. The evidence regarding the presence of accused 785 6 along with accused 7 and PW. 1 near about a scene where there was a dispute over the deceased wives of A 1 on account of which some persons were involved, was disbelieved by the Sessions Judge who found that only two persons were required for an offence of conspiracy under section 120A I.P.C., to be constituted in respect thereof. In view of the acquittal of all seven accused by the trial court of charge framed under section 302 read with section 34 I. P.C. and the confirmation of conviction and sentence awarded to accused 1, S, S and S.S. was set aside. The High Court allowed the appeal filed by accused 2 and 6 and acquitted him of that charge. Hence the appeals. Dismissing the appeals, the Court ^ HELD: 1(i) The retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 4 in this case in view of section 32 of the Indian Penal Code and no appeal was filed in this Court against the acquittal by accused B.

The appellant 's property was sought to be sold by the respondent I on August 22, 1945. The recitals in the will clearly and specifically stated that the testatrix had the knowledge of the contents of the Will; that after her death the document would remain with the appellant and it added that the plaintiff had not executed any prior will but that in case any such will has been executed by her the same stood cancelled by the execution of the present will; and on the evidence, the sound and disposing state of mind. The High Court held that even if it had found in favour of the appellant on these two points it would not have been of any help to him because his case must inevitably fail when it is held that the will set up by him was not proved to be the last will and testament of Lakshmamma. Held, further, that after the fact that the testator was ill at Mandya and had received substantial benefit under the will and since the appellant had taken a leading part in its execution, the onus was heavy on him to remove the suspicions attending execution of a document and to establish that the executant fully understood the nature of the recitals in his preamble and the effect of the dispositions before she put her signature to the document of his own free will. The fact that after his death the testatrix has not executed anything more than an act of undue influence can not exonerate him of any possible doubt. There may be other suspicious circumstances attending on the execution. It may, however, be stated generally that a propounder of the will has to prove the due and valid execution of his will and that if there are any suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution must remove those doubts from the mind of the court by cogent and satisfactory evidence. The propounder would be called upon to show by satisfactory evidence that the document so propounded is the last Will of a free and capable testator 's signature on it when she was in a sound disposing state or of mind as required by law, courts would be justified in making a finding in favour Of the propounder.

The appellants were selling Arcons known as "Cinema Arc Carbons" manufactured by the appellant company, which was used in the manufacture of Arcobons. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed an application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether are carbons manufactured by it could be covered by the entry under consideration. It further held that the use which is generally made of the arc carbonons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. The High Court also dismissed the appeal without taking further evidence. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the word "electrode" to describe them, suggesting a connection with electricity, nor their utilisation in a process involving application of electrical power could convert them into "electrical goods" as contemplated by the Entry in the Madras Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The term "accessories" is used in several entries such as entry No. 6 for clocks, time pieces and watches, Entry No. 10 for dictaphones and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and Entry No 11 for sound transmitting equipment such as telephones and loud speakers. Our object in indicating the nature of entries, amdist which entry No 4 occurs, is to show that some precision has been attempted in making the entries. When it was intended to confine the entry to particular gadgets and "parts thereof" the entry said so. Of course, even where an entry relates to parts manufactured for use for a particular kind of instrument of gadget only, the article manufactured to serve as a part of a particular type of apparatus would not cease to be covered under the intended Entry simply because a purchaser makes some other use of it. [564B C] The Andhra Pradesh High Court correctly held that "the main use of the are carboons under considerment" was duly established to be the purpose of production in the projectors or other cinematographic equipment.

Section 15 of the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966 empowers the Central Government to enhance or reduce the rate of royalty prescribed by the Second Schedule in respect of any mineral subject to the condition that the Central Govern ment shall not enhance the rate Of royalty in respect thereof. The Act was passed in the year 1957 by Parliament to provide for the regulation of mines and development of minerals under the control of the Union and it was made applicable to the whole of India. Under section 3A of the Act, the words 'minerals ' were defined as including all minerals except mineral oils. Clause (e) of the said section defines minor minerals ' as building stones etc., gravel, ordinary sand other than sand used for prescribed purposes and any other mineral which the Central Govt may by notification in the Official Gazette declare to be a minor mineral. The petitioners challenged the validity of Rule 21 on various grounds, namely: 1. that the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the State the levy is bad; and 2. that in any event the impugned notification was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1(a) The impugned Rule 21 which was substituted in the place of the former rule 21 was invalid as it was discriminatory in character. [415G] (b). In view of the decision of this Court in B.K. Trivedi & Sons and Ors. vs State of Gujarat and ors., ; , the validity Of the Rules made thereunder had been considered and the contentions urged by them against the said rule in those petitions, had been rejected in the present case. [413G] The levy is ex ceived under a law made by the Central Gov ernment on which alone the restriction contemplat ed under Article 304(b) applies. It is not an imposition made by a law or by the authority on which it alone the restrictions contemplat ing under Article 709 of the Constitu tion regarding movement of goods from one State to another for the activity of quarrying does not involve any movement as such. [414B] (c). The levy in question is ex facie ordo ned and has been imposed in an arbitrary manner. The burden of establishing that the levy was unreasonably heavy, is on the petitioners. It can be urged that the impugned Rule is challeng ing the power or the power which has been conferred by it. [416C] (d). Section 15 of Part II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution does not authorise the State Government to show such con tention while promulgating the Rules which are in the nature of subordi nate legislation is also of no consequence. The levy was arbitrarily imposed. It was obvious that the petitioners were lessees who are exploiting the mining areas for purposes of business and that the royalties in question are ultimately passed on to the consumers. It cannot be said that the business is adversely affected in such a way that it is liable to be struck down on the ground of arbitrariness. [411C E] In the instant case, the levy in questo nent to show concession while promulging the Rules does not specifically authorise the state Government to make such discrimination. The power exercised is legislative in character and the authority which is exercising the said power has the power to make rules equi table by necessary implication.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village at a meeting held on June 27, 1957. According to the appellant the temple was rounded two hundred years ago by the members of his community and since then the management of the temple and is affairs was always vested in the community of the Sangunatha Ammal Community and no person other than the elected trustee had at any time the right of management and control of the Temple. The appellant contended that the temple being rounded two thousand years ago, by the member of his Community and since thereafter the management was always vests in the Community of the Community and there was no person who other than his elected trustees had at all time the rights of management, and control and of the deity. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. On appeal, the High Court set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge but allowed the appeal and set aside that of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that the succession is "regulated by usage" and therefore the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 1 of 1925; (ii) that in view of the provisions of the Act, the appellant is not a hereditary trustees within the contemplation of section. HELD: (1) The word "succession" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". [445 B] State of Madras vs Ramakrishna, ; , followed. (2) It is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. It is quite possible that for that vacancy A himself might be reelected because a retiring trustee is eligible for reelection. The possibility of A being the successor A himself is not merely an anomaly, it is an impossible legal position. No man can succeed to his own office. In Black 's Law Dictionary the word "Succession ' is defined as follows: "The revolution of title to property under the law of descent and distribution". [427 C] State Of Madras vs Rama, ; followed.

On hearing the shout of his deceased brother crying "younger brother: Bonus Mohan Krishnan is running after stabbing me with knife 'catch him ', and in court he ran to his elder brother who came from the side of the bench where he was lying dead. The appellant asked the deceased to lodge the information report in the police Station, which was very close to the places where he fell dead. The doctor (PW 16) who held the postmortem examination found nine injuries two of which were incised and four as punctured incised, two more as regulated and the remaining one as a vertical incised wound. The High Court relying on the evidence of these eye witnesses, namely, PWs 1 3 and 5 who were eye witnesses and described them as "a bunch of liars", "unashamed liars and coparcurers". On appeal by special leave, it was contended that there was a mention about a pool of blood only where the dead body was found at No.1 in the FIR stands contradicted by the testimony of PW 4 and that the High Court erred in convicting the appellant on the sole testimony of P 's son (reasedii) who gave him a "candid, natural and truthful version. , therefore, there has been a long history of bitter feabbing over nearly two decade between his first accused and his son on the other". Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. There was no difficulty in adopting that course in this case where the testimony o sole witness has been rejected with reference to the first accused who was on the same boat with the appellant. [711G] 2.1 In a given case, there is no mention about any pool of evidence of blood even where the deceased died at No 1 in the same site plan.

The respondents who had a firm of solicitors were partners in a firm. The firm kept its accounts on cash basis and the amount was paid after his death but before he was assessed, they filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and then to the Tribunal. The question was whether the income received subsequent to the previous year in which Amarchand died was liable to be assessed to income tax under section 24B(1) of the Income tax Act for the assessment years 1950 51, 1951 52, 1952 53, 1953 54 and 1954 55. Held, that the fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three subsections of section 24 B and cannot be extended beyond that legitimate field. In re Sreemati Usharani Shoudhurani, , referred to. In the present case the amounts which were sought to be taxed and which have been held not to be liable to tax were those which were not received in the previous years and were therefore not liable to income of the heirs and legal representatives who cannot be deemed to be assessees for the purpose of assessment in regard to these years,.[708 C D] In re. Srelaatsu Areas & Co., Ltd. vs Commissioner of Income tax Bombay City, , applied. Bengal Immunity Co. Ltd.v. The State of Bihar, [1942] 14 I.T.R. 10, distinguished. In Re Srememati Sehlani Shudhurani and Co. vs The Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay City. ; , at p. 106 it was observed that the question whether a particular amount was income or not had nothing to do with the time of its receipt and the question of receipt was material only for the purposes of determining whether on that amount tax was to be levied under the Act in the year of assessment. The expression 'if he had not died ' means that irrespective of the date of ' receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income is received by his heirs and Legal representatives after his heirs his death they are liable for payment of the tax just as the deceased would have been liable when the income was received had he been living.

The petitioners, who were appointed directly by promotion or by transfer to posts reserved under the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959, challenged the Act and the proposed action as ultra vires the Constitution. The contentions raised before the High Court were: (i) That Article 16(3) of the Constitu tion which provides for equality of opportunity in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State, is constitutionally valid; (ii) that the word 'State ' here was to be understood in the extended meaning given to it by the definition of that word article 12. The legislative power to create residential qualification for employment is thus exclusively conferred on Parliament; Parliament can make a law which prescribes. any requirement as to residence within the State or Union territory prior to appointment or appointment, to an office in that State orUnion territory prior thereto or appointment. (iii) It has already made a declaration that no person shall be disqualified for any office in the territory of India because of his residence in any particular part of India. The contention of the petitioners was that the State Legislature, while prescribing the requirement, may prescribe the requirements of residence in a particular part in passing the Constitution, has not dealt with such an objection; (iv) That the requirement might be also as to resided under the Union Territory or part of that State and, therefore, Parliament is supreme and can make any law on the subject as the Article says. (v) The words 'any requirement ' cannot be read to warrant something which could have been said more specifically. The word 'state ' here is to be construed in the wider sense of the ordinary meaning given by the expression in that article, whereas there may be no discrimination among other things on the ground of residence. Realising therefore, that sometimes local sentiments may have to be respected or sometimes an inroad from more advance States into less developed States may have had to be prevented and a residential qualification may, therefore have to he prescribed, the exception in clause (3) was made. Even so, that clause speaks of residence within State. The claim of Mr. J. Das seeking to put a very wide and liberal construction upon the words ' any requirement ' can be read into warrant something. which could not have been so more specifically; These words bear on the kind of residence or its duration rather than its location within the state. (vi) That cl. 3 confers an additional right on Parliament to make laws for the further implementing of the law made by Parliament is valid and not. The requirement cannot be treated as reasonable.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of them he was charged with offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him in each of the three appeals for offences tinder section 52. On appeal by the State it was contended that the search was illegal inasmuch as it was in contravention of the provisions of sections 103 and 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held, that the prosecution had failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant. The mere fact that there is even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission. It is common experience that delivery of postal articles is now and again delayed for a considerable length of time may be through accident or through the negligence of the postal employees. It was probably for this reason that the definition clearly lays down that until an article despatched by post is delivered or can be said to be delivered that it will be deemed to be In course of trans portation by post from the time of its being delivered to a Post Office to the time when its being actually delivered to the sender or otherwise disposed of under Chapter VII. The object of the provision was to prevent postal articles 'in course of the transmission by post 'from being tampered with, and so the secreting, destruction etc., of postal article would frustrate or tend to frustrate their delivery to the addressees.

Under section 85 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947, the Sarpanch and the Pan chas had knowledge of the order. The High Court held that the Nyaya Panchayats exercised judicial powers and even if a Panchas had knowledge that the District Magistrate was not satisfied for want of evidence by way of proper affidavit etc., the Nyaya Panchayat had rightly dismissed the application. On appeal to this Court it was contended : (i) that the procedure adopted by the Gram panchs in not doing so was really not bona fide; (ii) that even if the Panchas did not believe the contents of the application, and affidavit of the party that the High Court had stayed further proceedings before the Panchayat, nor was there any thing in the order sheet to show that the Panchas did not belief he bad the contents. HELD : (1) Where a person bona fide comes to the conclusion on the material placed before him that the source of information is not authentic he cannot be held guilty of contempt of court for disobeying the order.[119 C E] (2)(a) The High court 's finding that the Sarpanch had knowledge over the copy of the telegram was not recorded and only copy of an telegram was produced. It was no part of the duty of the Pan COcha to enquire from the S.D.M about the filing of the original application before him. At any rate, he has apparently no jurisdiction to stay proceedings before them when no proceeding is pending before him.[119 E F] (b) There is no such evidence in this case. [119 F G] (d) It is not proved on record that any such application was made by the Sarpanch to the Gram Panchs of the Panchayat which was merely an affidavit sworn to before a person authorised to administer oaths. It be true that in some cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of Court.[120 E F G].

The appellant was charged with murder of a person who was sleeping in his cattle shed in village Bhadurpur Ghar, with a sword at about mid night on the night between June 14 15, 1960. The prosecution case was that due to enmity, the appellant caused injuries to Sheo Sahai and asked him to go to the Police Station, Ekdil, nine miles away and lodged a report. He delivered the sword which had been found by the Serologist to be stained with human blood. The appellant was taken in custody and as a result of investigation was sent up for trial, The appellant denied the allegation that he had caused the death of Sheo Sahai. The Sessions Judge believed Ujagar Singh 's statement about the appellant 's confessing to him that he did commit the murder of Sheo Swarup Sahai and that he deposited it stained with his human blood at the Police station on the day of the murder. The High Court, however, did not rely on this extra judicial confession. It relied on certain statements made by the appellant in his report dictated at the police Station and considered those facts together with the motive and the evidence about the purchase of the sword sufficient to confirm the appellant his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the entire report dictated by the appel lant was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the accused made to a Police Officer and that the evidence relied upon by the High Court was insufficient to establish conclusively that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai, and that there were good reasons for Ujagar Singh not leaving his field whose crops he was watching against the neel gais. HELD: (i) The extra judicial confessions are not usually considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person whom who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement should not be believed. [206 E] (ii) It may be that having blurted out the truth to be proceeded to the police station and report the matter there, there is no reason for a person 's acting in a certain manner. It may also be that taking blurtling out the falsehood to Ujagar Singh, when taken by surprise, the appell lant thought the best thing to be to proceed to the nal police station, and report about it.

% The respondents in c.A. 1640/79 challenged the electoral roll of the appellants by way of an election petition before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur on December 28, 1978 requesting the court to make an order quashing the electoral rolls and the calendar of events issued for the purpose of the election and directing the respondent not to notify the results of the Election under Rule 46 of the Rules pending disposal of the writ petition. A Division Bench of the High court dismissed the petition holding (i) that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation Act, 1956; and (ii) that even though an assessment was made by the Deputy Collector with regard to the irregularity in the division of Raipur town into different wards for purposes of election. On appeal, this Court by its order dated December 31, 1978 allowed the appeals, setting aside the electoral Roll and directing that the Panchayat Constituency Election Officer shall abide by it expeditiously, which was done on November 16, 1978. The High Court dismissed the writ application holding (1) that respondent No. 2, the Deputy Collec tor had asked them to appear before him on October 30, l4 1978 and that as he did not produce any evidence in support of his claim, his application was rejected; and and (2) that inspite of the aforesaid interim order made by this Court, a large number or people who could have filed claims and objections were prevented from preferring them within the 30 days from the date of publication of the notice under rule 46 of tO the Rules within which the claims and objection could be preferred and in paragraph 7 thereof it had been stated that any such claim or objection filed beyond the prescribed period was liable to be rejected. The respondent company and its directors were prosecuted under sections 32(5) and 133(3) of the Companies Act, 1913 for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of that Act. The High Court acquitted the directors holding that if no balance sheet was laid before a general body meeting nor could it be so laid, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and though wilful omission to call a general Body meeting and lay the balance sheets and profit & loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly does not make him liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of Companies Act 1913 or section 220 of the . In appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The holding of the annual general meeting and the laying before it of the balancesheet and profit account is a sine qua non for filing of the copies thereof before the Registrar. If no such balance sheet is laid before the general body, there could be no objection to that balance sheets not being utilised nor of compliance with the provisions contained in any of the four preceding sub sections. [416 A] (2) The finding of the High Court that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one also shows that the obligation to file the list is independent of the holding of a general meeting. [417 B C] (3) Under section 134 the laying of a balance sheet or profit and losses account before the company in the general meeting is made obligatory. Under section 133 the failure to comply with section 131 is made punishable. But section 134 lays down that after balance sheet, and profit loss account or the income and expenditure account as the case may be, have been laid before it at a general Meeting three copies thereof shall be filed with the registrar, and a failure to do so is made penal by the Act. [414 C] Gibson vs Barlon, ; , followed. (4) The liability of sending three copies of the Balance sheet and profits and loss accounts which are laid before such general body may have been forwarded under sub section (1), of section 132 cannot be complied with. While the appeal to a question of principle might be attractive, it cannot ignore the clear words of the section. Where the words of a section are very clear it is unnecessary to consider whether it embodies any principle and whether that principle is consistent with the principle as embodied a certain other sections which are differently worded. In interpreting a penal provision it is not permissible to give an extended meaning to the plain words of that section on the ground that a principle recognised in respect of certain other provisions Of law requires that this section should be interpreted is the same way. [413 D E] (5) The court there observed that the decision in Park vs Lawton, ; and Park vs lawton, , referred to.

The respondent and 49 other persons were charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by them in the course of their raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum Dum, and they were convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprison ment by the Special Court to which the case was sent for trial by the Governor of West Bengal by a notification dated 26th January 1950. The respondent applied to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the conviction and sentence on the ground that the Special judge had no jurisdiction to try the case inasmuch as section 5 (1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1949, was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitu tion in so far as it purported to vest in the State Government an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial "any cases ", which must include an individual case, "whether the duration of such a case is likely to be long or not ". The High Court quashed the conviction. Held, that section 5(1) Of the WestBengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949 was valid as it did not by itself make any distinction between cases and offences triable by the special court and those for the purpose of being tried by a Special Court. The classification implied in this part of the sub section had no reference to, and was not directed towards the singling out of any particular person as an object of hostile State action but was concerned only with the grouping of "offences", "classes of offences" and "cl classes of cases".

The appellant was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of textiles. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the business which had been subjected to tax under the Act of 1918 had ceased at any time before 1948 or (b) whether there was a succession by another person for the person who was carrying On April 1, 1939, and therefore, the partnership business continued in the hands of the same person who had paid tax under section 25(4). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner also held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 26 (2) of the Income tax Act. The Tribunal however held that on May 30, 1939 there was discontinuance of the business within the meaning of section 25 (3) and that the partnership in question had been discontinued in October/November 1937 or on May 31, 1939 and it was not in existence in 1948 so as to permit a succession to it taking place under the instrument of February 7, 1948. The High Court held that there was no succession within the mischief of section 26(2) and therefore the partnership firm could be said to have ceased at the date of the partition and on such discontinuance the family became entitled to relief under s.25 (4). Held, that the question whether there has been a succession within section 26 or for the purpose of section 24 (4) was one of fact and not of law and must be decided on its own facts. The business which was taxed under the Income Tax Act of 1922 had ceased to exist before the benefit of section25 (3). The business in question was carried on by a person different from those who carried it on as a whole. The partnership was brought about by the instrument Of December 6, 1918 for the partners in the two firms were not the same. There was no cessation of business in so far as the original business of piece goods, yarn and banking was concerned. That business continued even in the possession of the firm after the partition of the partnership. The firm had been dissolved in October, 1943 or on June 30, 1940, and it could not be said that the same business on which tax had been charged under the 1922 Act of 1947 had ceased. Held, further, that there could be no question of the succession to the business carried on at the commencement of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939 in so as the partnership was concerned because the firm was dissolved and it had been continued by two independent firms for the document of October 30, 1943, which was a complete change of ownership of all the businesses was necessary for purposes of section 23(2), before it could be held that it was the business of the partners that was carried in by the firm as a result of a transfer by an instrument executed on February 7. The fact that he was not taken on in the original partnership business also shows that the original firm business in respect of which alone the benefit had been claimed by one of the members of the erstwhile family and not by the whole family, though I express no opinion upon it, but even so that would be a case of succession rather than of discontinuance. The mere fact that the assessee was not taking on in April 1 1939, did not make any difference because the original assessment year was not a dissolution of the original one of 1947 and 1948.

The appellant 's suit based as it was on the provisions of section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, was essentially a claim to obtain a share in the interest which her husband had at the time of his death in the coparcenary property. Two things became necessary to determine for the purpose of giving relief to the plaintiff. One, her share in her husband 's share and two, her husband, 's own share in a coparcenary property, were thus clears : One, that in a partition between Khandappa and his two sons, there would be four sharers in the joint family properties, the fourth being Khandappa 's wife, the plaintiff 's son, and their two children each having a 1/4th share therein. Adding 1/3rd and 1/24th, the appellant claims a 7/24 th share in one of the joint families. The other three getting 1/2 share each would devolve upon his death on six sharers, the other being Khandappappa ' 's 1/6th share would devolve on his death. On the question whether the plaintiff was entitled to a 7 /24th share by ignoring the 1/5th share which she would have obtained had there been a partition during her husband life time between him and his sons. HELD : (1) The view taken by the Bombay High Court in Rangubai Lalji vs Laxman Lalji, [1959] Stipp. 1 S.C.R. 394, that Explanation 1 to section 6 does not apply, that the proviso to that section is attracted and that the decision of the appeal must turn on the meaning to be given to Explanation 1 of section6. The interpretation which will further the intention of the legislature and remedy the injustice from which the Hindu women have suffered over the years, is truly to permit one 's imagination to boggle under the oppression of the reality that there was in fact no partition between the plaintiff and his coparceners immediately before his death, and that assumption, having been made once for the purposes of ascertaining the share of the deceased in the coparcener property, one cannot go back on that assumption and ascertain the share Of the heirs without reference to it. [765 E F] (2) The plain meaning of Explanation 1 is the subject matter of acute controversy between the parties. The plaintiff ' s suit based on the provision of section 30 of the Act was essentially one claim to recover a share from the defendant. The proviso to section six comes into play and the normal rule is excluded. [766 G] (3) The interpretation that Explanation I has to be read as enabling a person who has separated himself from the coparcenary before the death of the person in whose property the heirs claim a share. The fiction created by Explanation 1 has to he given its due and full effect as the fiction created under section 18A(9)(b). [767 A] (4) The assumption that Explanation1 has to have been given its true effect is not a processual step devised merely for the limited purpose of working out some other conclusion. It has to, be treated and accepted as a concrete reality, something that cannot be recalled just as a share allotted to a coparcener in an actual partition cannot generally be recalled.

(2) The High COurt proceeded on the basis that the allegations in the letter were not disputed and challenged. The petitioner company was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act. Suraj Mall Mohta was also the managing director of another company Messrs. Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. A reference had been made by the Central Government under section 5(1) of the Act before 58 450 1st September, 1948, of the case of the petitioner along with the cases of Suraj Mall Keta and other members of his family may be referred to the Commission for investigation. On the 15th of September, 1953, a report to this effect was made by it to the Central Govern ment under section 6(1), requesting that the case be investigated and they were called upon to furnish certain material as detailed in Annexure "B" of the petition, to the petitioner. On 12th April 1954, the Commission notified the petitioners that their cases had been referred for investigation and they should furnish certain materials as detailed therein. The present petition under article 32 of the Constitution was filed for the issue of appropriate writs restraining the Commission from taking any action against the petitioner under the provisions of the , on the ground that the provisions Of sections 5(4), 6, 7 and 8 of the Indian Income tax Act had become void being discriminatory in character after the coming into force of the constitution of India. Held, that section 5 (1) Of the Indian Incometax Act and sub section (4) of section 5 of the impugned Act deal with all persons who have similar characteristics and similar properties, the common characteristics being that they are persons who had not truly disclosed their income and have evaded payment of taxation on income. It is not possible to hold that all such persons who evade payment of income tax and come within the ambit of section 34 of the Income tax ' Act and come under it, but without in any way deciding or even expressing any opinion on that question, they cannot be dealt with under the provi sions of section 4 Of the impugned act. The respondent, a company registered under section 26 of the Indian Companies Act 1913, was carrying on business in matters of inland and foreign trade. The primary objects of the Federation as given in the Memorandum of Association are "regulation of hours of work, payment of wages, leave, holiday terms of service and other conditions of work of persons employed in shop commercial establishment, establishments for public entertainment or amusement and other establishments and to provide for certain matters connected therewith". Section 1(4) indicates its extent and application. It shall apply in the first instance only to the municipal areas, notified areas of Delhi and New Delhi etc., but Government may by notification extend or apply it to shops and establishments in the other local area or areas. The definitions of " commercial establishment" and "shop" given in sub sections (5), (9) and (27) of section 2 are material for our purpose. They read " Commercial Establishment" means any premises wherein any trade, business or profession is carried on, or (b) any work in connection with, or incidental or ancillary thereto is carried On and includes a society registered under the , and charitable or other trust, whether registered or not which carries on any business, trade or profession. " Establishment" mean any premises where goods are sold, either by retail or wholesale Or where services are rendered to customers, and includes an office, a stoic room, godown, warehouse or work place, whether in the same premises or otherwise used in connection therewith or in connection With such trade or business but does not include a shop or a factory registered under tho , or theaters, cinemas, restaurants eating houses, residential hotels, clubs or other places of public amusement or entertainment. " establishment" means a shop, a commercial establishment and a residential hotel, restaurant, eating house, theatre or other place of public entertainment to which this Act applies and includes such other establishment as Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be an establishment for the purposes of the Act. " Commercial establishment" is defined in section 2(5) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. The main object of the said Act as stated in its preamble is "regulation for hours of business, payment, of wages etc., of persons engaged in shop, commercial establishments, establishments, for public institution or amusement or other establishments". Section 2(7) defines 'establishment ' to mean any building where goods were sold, whether by retail, wholesale or where services were rendered to customer. The definition of "commercial establishment" includes a shop and a commercial Establishment. The term "shops" is wide enough to include the idea of profit, yet the definition of the mere word "trade" does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. But putting aside the question whether they carry on a trade, how can it be denied that the Council carry on business. They are incorporated; they have a secretary and they print books, they sell those books, them do all that is ordinarily done in carrying on the business of a bookseller. The mere fact of the matter is that the respondent is a Federation of Federations and not an association of any individual traders, industrialists or businessmen. As regards the preliminary objection, it was held by this Court that the activity of the Association amounts to "work in connection" with, inter alia, of "industry" as defined in s.2(j) of ' the Act, which in consequence had no application. From the side of the present appellant, at first a half hearted attempt was made to show that the Federation is carrying on a profession as it is "tendering advice to all businessmen and traders". This contention was negatived by this court in Management of the Union of the India Chamber of Commerce and Industry vs Their workmen, Shri R. K. Mittal, [1971] 1 S.C.R. No. 869.

The respondent assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. The village of Benares loaded with Jagir became payable by the Zamindars direct to the Government. By this arrangement the revenue or land collections of Jagir became available by the jagirdar from year to year by the grant of the pension, Babu Hat Narain Singh and his successors no longer remained the proprietors of the Parganas or the jagir and became entitled to merely a pension. The letter written by which the amount of pension was determined at Rs. 36,322/8 is dated July 7, 1837 and was from H. Elliot Esqr., the Secretary to Lt. Government, N.W.P. Allahabad to J. Thompson Esq. Lt. Governor of Government, therefore, held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. The source of the salary was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of income was not land or rent collections from land, it is difficult to hold that the receipt of the respondent was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. The High Court held that from the language of the letter of July 7 18 37, it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. On appeal by special leave: HELD: (1) In this case the source of 'of income is clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 which and therefore it is not agricultural income as defined in the Act, [705 G; 704 A] (2) The allowance was revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. [706 C] State of Uttar Pradesh vs Kunwar Sri Trivendram Narain. Singh, ; , followed.
