The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and some other private operators filed writ petitions in the High Court. The High Court set aside a grant of three out of eleven permits to the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation and enhanced the number of permits granted to the private operators from one to three. The Tribunal took the view that having regard to the rule of preference enunciated by proviso to section 63(7) and the applications from the 'non preferred ' category had to be excluded as the number Of applications from applicants who were required to be given preference exceeded the number specified in the application for permits to be granted, and held that after considering the claims of the eligible applicants in the manner indicated in Sher Singh 's case and examining the merits of the claims, the applications became entitled to be included. It was, therefore, directed that the State Transport Appellate Tribunal should dispose of the applications afresh in accordance with law, after considering all the claims raised by the applicants without waiting for any further appeal, and after giving a personal hearing to the eligible applicant. The Karnataka State Transport Corporation appealed to this Court for relief by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The general scheme of the Act in the matter of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the case of a notified route or notified area, where under section 68 F(1) the permit has to be necessarily granted to tile State Transport Undertaking, in all other cases, the claims Of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits, applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. Except in the cases of a specified notified route, the application of no applicant may be altogether excluded from consideration on the sole ground that another applicant is entitled to preference under one or the other provisions of the statute. The proviso to about section 63 (7) specifically provides that other conditions being equal, an application for stage carriage permit from a State Transport undertaking for operating in any interState route shall be given priority over all other applications. While it is true that section 47(1 H) does not expressly refer to "other things being equal", it appears to him, be implicit in the provision that other things are equal. The rule is a rule of caution and if the discretion to grant approval is to be exercised once the minimum conditions are fulfilled. [1015 A C] 2.1 There is no question of eliminating private operators merely because the Undertaking applies for a stage carriage permits under Chapter IV, it must satisfy the Regional Transport Authority that it is better suited than the private operator to render transport facility to the travelling public. The scheme makes no reference to the proviso to Section 63(1).

The respondent purchased, by a registered instrument dated October 5, 1956, the business carried on by one Purushottam Raju under the name All India Trading Company. Purushottam Raju was the sole proprietor of the business and had been assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The assessee paid some amounts towards sales tax thus determined but there remained some arrears of sales tax i.e., Rs. 3836 4 0 for 1948 49, and Rs. 1218 1 9 for 1949 50, and for 194950. The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the said business. The respondent 6 63 denied liability to pay sales tax but his contention was over ruled by the Deputy Commercial Tax Officer. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the orders of the Commercial Tax officer and the Board of Revenue. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Government under sections 19(1) and 19(2)(c) of the Act, and that the respondent was not liable to pay the sales tax due from his predecessor in title, Purushottam Raju. This appeal is brought by special leave. HELD: The word 'assessment ' used in section 19(l)(c), does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule is beyond the rule made power of State Government either under section 19 (1) or section 19 or section19(2) (c) or of the Central Act. [665 B] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, , Chatturam vs C I.T. Bihar, ; Chattaram vs C .I. T. Bihar; , Chattyuram vs Commissioner of Inland Revenue, ; and Chattramuram vsC.I., Bihar; referred to.

The appellant entered service in the Gondal State. In 1927, he was suspended and at that time he was acting as Accountant at Rajkot Central Prison, and on March 7, 1954, he had committed certain acts of mis appropriation of food stuffs meant for prisoners maltreatment of prisoners and acceptance of illegal gratification from them, but on enquiry held by him, the police found that the appellant 's conduct amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311(2) of the Constitution. The appellant 'reprehensible action taken against him in respect of arrears of pay from April 1, 1954 to May 7, 1956. He filed a written statement contending that the departmental enquiry was vitiated as he had not been furnished with copies of the report of the Enquiry Officer, and that the Inspector General of Prisons had recorded before him and the tentative conclusions arrived at by the Enquiry officer were bound to influence him, and in depriving them of a copy of the same he was handicapped. The High Court held that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the appellant with a copy, of the enquiry report amounted to violation of article 311 (2) Of the Constitution, as according to it there was no duty to supply a copy thereof and had not prejudiced by the non supply of the copy of his report. Held, that though some elements of relationship existed between a public servant and Government servants, the liability to pay wages when it has been fixed arises out of a contract to pay salary, is not lacking even in England where a special relationship exists between the Crown and its public servants. In the present case, however, some elements were of relationship which arose between the appellant and Government were based on contract within the meaning of section 60 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, and the liability arising out of them was one of damages. The decree of the High Court decreeing payment of arrears was truly a liability in proceedings relating to a contract within section 60(2)(a) of that Act rather than under section 61.

The appellant 's predecessor in interest, was granted a mining lease of the coal and coal mining rights in respect of 300 bighas out of his 400 bighas to one P. W. No. 1. When P executed a lease of 1928, I instituted a suit for conversion of property on the northern boundary of P.W. 3(b) from another plot of 96 bighas to another plot. The plaint was based on the following allegations: (a) that the southern boundary of the appellant ' s leasehold is conterminous with the northern boundaries of the respondents ' lease hold; (b) that as a result of a letter written by the Inspector of Mines on August 18, 1941, the plaintiff made an inquiry and came to know that the defendants had encroached upon their coal mines on the southern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. On those allegations, they asked for the following reliefs: (i) That the intermediate boundary line between the appellant and P; and (ii) that a permanent injunction be issued against the defendants restraining them from encroaching upon the appellants ' coal land and cutting and removing coal therefrom. Held, that the suit was for conversion to property and the question of limitation as framed by section 100 of the Indian Evidence Act would not survive in the present case. Under section 101 of the Evidence Act the burden in the former sense is on the party who comes to court to get a decision on the existence of certain facts which he asserts. In the instant case, P proved that the knowledge of his father was within three years of the suit and that the entire burden was on the plaintiff in these suits to prove that he obtained the knowledge thereof by examining the school records and having considered the extent of land being thereby unworkable is entirely lost to them for ever. It was not necessary for him to prove this part in the plaint which was beyond three years from the date when they had knowledge of it. Talyarkhan vs Gangadas, (1920) L.R. 59 I.A. 588 and Sundarji Shivji vs Secretary of State for India, [1939] F.C.R., p. 751, relied on. Held further, that in view of the finding of fact arrived at by the courts below in respect to this issue, the court must be held to have acted affirmatively. No other point was raised and it was not a pure question of law involved in the appeal.

The appellant, a saw mill carrying on business in Kozihkode in 824 the State of Kerala. One Sankaran was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. It is said that on June 21, 1958, Sankaran came drunk to them mill and abused the Engineer, the Secretary and others and threatened them with physical violence. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. The appellant served a charge sheet on Sankaran on June 24, 1958 acting out the above facts and asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of his grave indiscipline and misconduct. The Industrial Tribunal held that something seemed to have happened on the afternoon of June 21. 1958 but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. It further held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders. The Tribunal also pointed out that no attempt was made before it to defend the action taken under rule 18 (a) by proving the alleged misconduct. Two witnesses were produced before the Tribunal in connection with the alleged offence but the Tribunal did not rely on them on the ground that the important witnesses, namely, the Engineer Secretary and other members of the staff whose evidence would have been of more value had not been produced and no explanation had been given why they were not produced. The tribunal also pointed Out that no effort was made by it to prove which had actually happen. It also held that there was nothing for it to justify before the Industrial Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Industrial Court has the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(A). [826 C] (ii) The employer could defend the actions under r . 18(b) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there were in fact misconduct and therefore the action was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of the power conferred. But the Tribunal has pointed out, that the employer did not attempt to do so before it. It satisfied itself by producing two witnesses but withholding the important witness on this question. [826 D] (iii) The industrial court in its opinion had the right of inquiring into the cause that might had led to the termination of services even under r, 18(c). But the tribunal has pointed Out, that it did not accept the evidence of the two witnesses who were produced, it cannot be said to have gone wrong. [827 E] (iv) The appellant failed to satisfy the Tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication that the exercise of power in this case was bona bonafide and was therefore not colourable. It could have easily done so by producing satisfactory evidence; but it seems to have rested upon its right that no such justification was required and, therefore, having failed to justify its action must suffer the consequences.

The appellants were the owners of a cinema theatre. The receivers granted a lease of the theatre on certain terms and conditions to two persons, Raval and Faraqui. By an agreement dated November 27, 1954, between Raval and Geneva, right to exhibit cinematograph films was granted to the latter on certain conditions. "Filmistan" instituted suit No. 149 of 1960 in the Court of Small Causes Ahmedabad against Raval and two other persons claiming a declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated October 27,1954 to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. By order dated December 1, 1960, the suit was disposed of as compromised. It was inter alia agreed that Raval and Cododod were bound and liable to allow Filmistan to exercise its "exhibition rights" in the cinema theatre; that Raval, and Fraqui, their servants and agents were not to have any right to exhibits any picture in contravention of the terms and condi tions of the agreement. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court set aside the order of the trial court and restored that of the Trial Court. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants: (1) that an enquiry into the nature of the legal relationship arising out of the document could be permitted to 'be put to the witnesses for Filmistans, and (2) that in any event the case or any part thereof was not likely to be disposed of on these issues. HELD : (i) The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. 442 This Court observed in Major section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 869 that the expression " case" is a word of comprehensive import and includes a civil proceeding and is not restricted by anything contained in section 115 of the Code to the entire proceedings in a civil court. To interpret the expression 'case ' as an entire proceeding only and not a part of the proceeding imposes an unwarranted restriction on the exercise of powers of superintendence and may result in certain cases in denying relief to the aggrieved litigant where it is most needed and may results in the perpetration of gross injustice. But it was not decided in Major s. Khanna vs Col. Brig. C. J Dillan, [1893] 1 K.B.D. 891, followed. (ii) The consent decree must be held to create a bar of res judicata as far as the question of document of November 27 is concerned. [436 E F] (iii) The Court gave no finding expressly or by implication on the issue of resjudicata or any other issue.

The respondent, a pilot Officer was granted a permanent commission in the Indian Air Force and was, therefore, inval idated from I.A.F. The Government of India issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The State of Uttar Pradesh also adopted the same scheme. Under that scheme the ex military official were appointed on contract basis for a fixed term which could be extended from time to time subject to the suitability of the official concerned but not beyond 58 years of age. Pursuant to the said scheme the respondent was appointed as Secretary in the District Soldiers Board in the district of Unnao in the State of U.P. The terms and conditions contained in the said order included the above term relating to the period of appointment and on his accepting the terms and condi tion he was appointed to the post till 30th August, 1985 and it was again extended upto 31st March, 1983 by an order dated 1st June, 1983. Again the term was extended upto 30th of August,1985 by an Order dated 1 6 1983. The respondent was required to furnish his acceptance of the terms & conditions contained therein includ ing the above terms relating to period of appoint ment and on accepting the term and conditions he was appoint ed as Secretary. The order was to be effective from the date of receipt of termination order and no charges were men tioned therein against the 1st respondent. The Respondent aggrieved by the said orders filed a Writ Petition before the High Court contending that he was entitled to salary upto the period he was enti tled to remain in service, i.e., 30th September, 1985 unless there was a further extension. But on 29.3.1985 the service of the 1 st respondent was terminated by the issue of a notice and payment of one month 's salary. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ petition was liable to be allowed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the interim order entitled him to be reinstated in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period beyond 30th 885 of August 1985. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has while setting aside the order of termination by its order dated 24.3 1988 directed that the respondent be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to con tinue till he completed the age of 58 years. Even the order passed on Review on 26.7.1988 does not make out that the Respondent had put forward at that stage such a case.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The Sessions Judge acquitted the accused but convicted him under section 307 Indian Penal Code. In appeal, in revision to the High Court, the appellant reiterated his plea that there was no reason to doubt the testimony of the prosecution witnesses which was supported by the medical evidence. He urged (i) that the discrepancies noticed by the Sessions Judge were of a minor character and they had been unduly magnified by the learned Sessions Judge; (ii) that there could be no reason for doubt the reliability of the evidence; (iii) that where two views of the witnesses are possible, the accused is entitled to the benefit of the doubt arising from the two views and that where the Trial Court has taken a possible view and acquitted the appellant, the High court should not interfere with the order of acquittal merely because another view was also possible. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(i) The principles are now well settled. At one time it was thou ht that an order of acquitting could be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial", and invite conclusions. However, the 'formula ' of "substantial & compelling reasons ' and the search for them were abandoned as a result of the pronouncement of this Court in Sanwat Singh 's case. Occasionally phrases like 'manifestly illegal ', grossly unjust ' have been used to describe the orders of acquittal which warrant interference. But it is essential that any view of the Evidence in favour of the accused must be reasonable even as any doubt, the benefit Of which an accused person may claim, must be a reasonable doubt. [368 G H] Sanwat vs Minister of pensions, ; , followed. 1096 (ii)(a) An order of discharge could be interfered with only where two substantial and compelling grounds out of conviction are possible. The principles laid down in San wat Singh ' 's Case may be added the further principle that "if two reasonable conclusions can be reached on the basis of the evi dence on record, the Appellate Court should not disturb the finding of the Trial court". [368 F G] Sanawat Singh & Ors. vs State of U.P., A.l. R. 1959 S.C., 460, applied.

The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court. He was convicted for having committed an offence under section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed his appeal and convicted him. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that (i) the President is given the power to appoint the Judges of the High Court as well as of the Chief Justice of the high Court by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with the Chief justice of India, the Governor of the State and in a case of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief Jus tice, the Chief Judge of a High Court can be removed from his office by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a minority of not less then two thirds of the members of that house present and voting, has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity; (ii) the power under clause (c) is the President and it is in this manner that section 6(1) (c), which specifically enjoins that no court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 161(or section 165 of the Indian Penal Code, or under sub section (2) or sub section 3A) of section 5 of this Act, alleged to have been committed by a public servant, except with the previous sanction, (a) in the case of any other person, of the authority competent to remove him from his Office; and (b) in case of a person who is employed in connection with the affairs of the Union and is not removable from his offices save by or with the sanction of the Central Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power to punish a High court Judge, if one may so describe it, is to be found only in article 2 read with Article 124(4) and (5) of Article 124 of the Constitution. [835C] 2.1 In the case, the President has not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge either of the, Supreme Court or of theHigh Court from his place in order to enable that authority to grant sanction for prosecution of the Judge under the provisions of section 6 of the Act and this can be done only if it is read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which such an opinion can be formed and there is no vertical superior with legal authority enabling obtaining of information from the concerned Judge. [889E] 2:2 The President, therefore, being the authority Competent to appoint and to remove Judge, of course in accordance with the procedure envisaged in Article 124, clauses (4) & (5), placed before the President, a Judge by warrant, under his hands and seal, after consultationwith such of the Judges. [879E F] 2 :3 The power of appointment and removal of a judge other than those of the highest Court is not contemplated by section 6, but only for the purpose of deciding whether the offence under clause(e) of possession of disproportionate assets which the Public servant cannot satisfactorily account is made out prima facie. [869C] 4:1. The President has no power or authority to remove any Judge either from his residence or from his post except with a previous sanction.

The respondent, a member of the Scheduled Caste, challenged the validity of the election on various grounds. At the hearing of the petition by the Election Tribunal the appellant contended that he was a Sunri by caste but was excluded from the Scheduled Castes group because he belonged to a smaller caste group of Sunirs known as Sahas. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the election petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was in error in interpreting the item on the evidence in the case as they appeared to have done, that there was no justification for doing that. After all, the evidence led in a case may be imperfect. Suppose the evidence, in another case led to the conclusion, as it might conceivably do do, that There was a smaller SC category within the Sunri caste of a person residing within the group of the Sunris. This is where the Tribunal went wrong and came to its conclusion that it had not been prov ed in this case that the appellant belonged to the smaller caste. [390G H] (2) The question now is, whether the respondent had established that the appel lant belonged to Scheduled Caste specified in item 40 of the President 's Order. To decide that point the description has first to be properly interpreted and understood, the Tribunal can ignore that construction of item 40 in the light of the evidence before it [390C F] (3) The expression "excluding Saha" meant excluding a smaller class group called Saha Sahas because the evidence on in the present case may conceivically do.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called "Ganga Vihar", Marine Drive, Bombay. The tenancy was a monthly one, the rent being Rs. 215. It is said that the appellant wanted to go to the United Kingdom for treatment of his failing eye sight and he got into touch with the police on 1 12 1948, and in conjunction with the latter, a trap was laid for the appellant. The complainant and the Sub Inspec tor were then taken to the appellant 's residence on 4 12 1948 and in connection with the raid held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of Rs. 30,500 from the rear seat of the car and also some papers, a typed draft of a partnership agreement was tween the complainant and his wife and the appellant, an application form for permission to occupy the building as caretaker. The appellant was charged under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, for receiving a pugree of Rs 29,500 and he was further charged under s 19(2) of that Act for receiving the said sum as a condition for the relin quishment of his tenancy. The defence of the appel lant was that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence, who was also to act as caRetaker of his flat anal that it was in this connection and with this object in view of his intended departure. The prosecution case was that the accused demanded a sum of RS. 30 lakhs which was later on reduced to Rs. 29, 500 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs 2,000 for the furniture, and that the complainant agreed to pay these sums. The wife of the deceased denied any aiding and abetting. The Presidency Magistrate who tried the case convicted him under section 19(1)(c) of 'the Act and sentenced him to one month 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs 30,000. The appeal preferred by the appellant was summarily dismissed on 20 2 1950. On 10 4 1950 the wife of appel late was acquitted, the evidence being insufficient to prove any abetment. The High Court rejected this contention on behalf of the appellants based on the language of section 19 (1) and this is the only point which required our consideration. Held:(i) An assignment of the lease or transfer in any other manner by a tenant is not made an offence; the statute merely says that it is not a lawful transaction. It was the landlord 's consent to the transfer of a lease by sub lease or otherwise on receipt of consideration that has been made an offen cientence. The section in question, it should be further noted does not speak of relinquishment or giving up of possession,in general terms. (ii) In the case of an assignment, the assignor contin ues to be liable to the landlord for the performance of his obligations under the tenancy and this liability is contrac tual, while the assignee becomes liable by reason of privity of estate. The consent of the landlord to an assignment is not necessary in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. But in the case Of relinquishment, it cannot be a unilateral transaction; it can only be in favour of the lessor by mutual agreement between them. (iii) In fact, a surrender or relinquishment terminates the lessee 's rights and lets in the lessor. It could only be made in favour o the lessor through mutual agreement. The relin cation of possession must be to the lessor or one who holds his interest.

The respondent companies/appellants in Civil Appeal No. 2299 of 1979 were engaged by the appellants, for the purpose of earning annual increments. The workmen on their own behalf had been granted various benefits such as dearness allowance and house rent allowance. Some time later they were revised. There was no separate dearness allowance until January, 1977 when it was introduced for the first time, and a flat increase from 15 years to 20 years in the span fell due to change in the basic pay scale with flat increases. Two days after the award was made, an application was made by the Union stating: "In view of the increased in the dearness allowance, the increase of Rs. 150/ to each workman in the category of Draftsmen and of Rs, 100/ to every employee in the other categories has been granted under my award. When the award is sent for publication, a necessary corrigendum be made in the award and the aforesaid words after figures Rs. 100 and Rs.100/ respectively have been added to the pay of each workman. The fitment has also to be done only after the flat increase is added to this basic salary of every employee. One is the retrospectivity attached to the revised wage scales, and the other is the flat increased increase given to each individual workman. It was contended that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis, and that it would not be possible for the respondent to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The Tribunal rejected the demand of the Unions for dearness allowance on the basis of a slab system because that would have imposed an unacceptable burden on the appellant 's financial capacity and there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in in the level of the basic wage. On appeal by special leave, it was contended: (1) The Tribunal erred in making the wage scales retrospective and in any event, in ranging the retrospectivity back to 1st January, 1976; (2) the amendment results in the inclusion of a flat increased of Rs 150/ and Rs 100/ (3) that there would be a resultant increase in the Dearness Allowance and house Rent allowance. [179 B D] The Industrial Tribunal on a consideration of the material placed before it came to the conclusion that the company was in an undoubted position to bear additional financial liability. The question is to what extent the relief should be given to the employees ? If without any flat or ad hoc increase of salary, the workmen were to be fitted into the revised scales of pay, it would obviously result in serious anomalous situations. [173 F H] 2(a) It is well settled that a liberal approach, which is adopted by Courts will not necessarily interfere with an award unless some other method is adopted. The court will take care of the principal and the entire circumstances of each case particularly those where there are many employees who may have been allowed to exercise their powers under section 17(1) of the Act even after they had exercised their authority in terms of section 17A of the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules. [174 A B] The decision of this Court in Tata Consulting Engineers first vs National Praxasi Mill Mazdoor Union ; distinguished. In the instant case, the Tribunal took note of the elaborate scales of wages already existing in the wage structure of the appellant and decided "to modify the existing structure of those scales with flat increase in each category". But it rejected the suggestion that a slab scheme should be introduced in the revising pay scale pertaining to different categories. The order dated December 22, 1978 of the Tribunal also does not reveal that there was any opposition by the company to the application for correcting the award.

The appellant, Sasamusa Sugar Works Ltd., and its workmen, the respondents an award had been made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/2/ per day, and in pursuance thereof, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the said award. This agreement was subsequently published in Bihar Gazette as a part of the award. In spite of the Award and the agreement, the appellant paid its employees only As. / 10/ per month and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The respondents contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal of the appel lant to pay to them wages at the rate awarded in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages, and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant to pay the said prescribed wages. The appellant raised two pleas against the respondents ' claim. It was urged that section 15 Of the Act was inapplicable because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section 2(vi) and it also argued, that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. The authority rejected the appellant 's contention and held that section 2 (vi) included wages prescribed under the Industrial Tribunal Act, and so it had rejected the appellants ' contention that the applications made by them were incompetent under section15 of the , and dismissed the petition. Held: (i) The basic assumption made by Mr. Setalvad in contending that section2(vi)(a) cannot take in the wages prescribed in the award is not well founded. When an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and its place is taken by the wage structures prescribed by it. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the parties, because that, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication. The true legal position is that when industrial disputes are decided by industrial adjudication and awards are made, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages fixed under the award cannot be treated as wages under section 2.(vi) of the Industrial Disputes Act before it was amended. (ii) The amendment has merely clarified what, in our opinion, was included in the unamended definition itself. In this connection, the South Indian Bank Ltd. vs A. R. Chacko, A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 1523, and V. B Godse, Manager, Prabha Mills Ltd., vs R. M. Naick Inspector, under the Payment of Wages Act, the Bombay High Court has interpreted section 2 of the . (iii) to include wages directed to be paid by industrial adjudica tion.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was charge sheeted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for forging the thumb impression of one Parma, and under section 408 he was acquitted by the trial Magistrate but convicted him both under section 465 and section 409 I.P.C. The High Court held that the charge under section 477 A required sanction as the official capacity was involved in the very act complained of as amounting to a crime; but after the disposal of the appeal by the High Court, it was discovered that there was no order sanctioning the prosecution and that the Chief Secretary had committed a mistake in sending up the communication. The appellant contended before this court that the sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for his prosecution was necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section 407(1). He relied on the decisions in Shreekantiah Ram Singh vs Emperor, [1948] L.R 75 I.A. 185 and R. W. Mathams V. State of West Bengal, (1950) L.L.R. 75 I A. 180; distinguished. Held further that sanction under Section 197(i) of Cr. P.C., for the prosecution was required as required by section 197 (1) Cr. The charge against the appellant did not fall within the scope of his duties and could be justified by him as done by virtue of his office. To claim to have paid the amount to Parma a token money as a public servant and to take his signature or thumb impression in acknowledgment thereof, the accused did not claim to had spent the amount in course of his official duties. The fact that he received a sum of Rs 51 alleged to have been misappropriated would not make out any offence under section 406 I. The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State as well as in what was British India and in Travancore State. It filed its income for the assessment year 1948 49, its accounting year being the previous calendar year. The Income tax Officer determined its assessable income to be Rs. 90 representing only the profit it made in Travancore state and under section 32(1) proviso (i) of the Travancore Act he refused a deduction of Rs. 79,275 shown as loss from branches situate outside the State. The assessee 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was unsuccessful but the Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that state. At the instance of the Commissioner of Income tax the following question was referred to the High Court of Travancore Cochin: " Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the loss of Rs 27,709 arising in Cochin State could be set off against the profit of Rs." The assessee contended that the first proviso to section 24(1)(i) did not apply to the head business business but only introduced an addendum that where the profits of the business arose in what is British India in the case of Travancore Act and the losses under the head 'business were sustained in an Indian State or in the latter case in any other Indian State, these losses could not by virtue of the proviso be deducted from profits made in British India or Travancore State as the case may be. Held, that the object of section 24 was to allow a set off of profits arising under different heads and only in such cases could recourse be had to section 25(1). Arunachalam Chettiar vs Commissioner of Incometax, Madras ([1950] S.C.R. 271), Ram Narain Sons Ltd. vs Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax (2) , distinguished.

The first respondent company was a Private Limited Company to take over the business of its partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace & Co. which had been doing business in India for about 60 years. In July, 1947, an agreement was entered into between the company and its employees at Calcutta under which, the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55. Subsequently, in September 1959, an arbitration award was passed fixing the age at 60 but the appellant Company challenged that award before the Industrial Tribunal by means of a writ petition. Thereafter the company resisted the workmen 's claim and contended that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had earlier been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees retirement at the age 60 subject to employees passing medical examination at reaching the 55 subject to their employee passing a Medical Examination on reaching an age of 55. The Tribunal held that this Court refused to disturb the award fixing the period of retirement at 60 years and, therefore, did not disturb the order fixing the retirement age at sixty60. It further directed that the age for workmen who were represented was fixed at 60 then, but the company could in its discretion and with the express or implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age, and it was entirely on the industry cum region basis. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The award and agreements on the question of age of superannuation about which information is furnished by several documents on this record clearly show a consistent trend in the Bombay region to fix the retirement Age of clerical and subordinate staff at 60 60. This was reasonable and unambiguous and they must be reasonably relied upon, namely, the observations made by this Court in Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs The Workmen ; , and Dunzmellop Rubber Company Ltd.,v. workmen and others; [427 E F] (ii) In spite of these infirmities the Tribunal took into account the fact that the Tribunal had found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region the trend had been to fix its retirement age on 60 years, but had brushed them aside in a way for which, on a closer examination it was clear that this document was of little assistance for finding out the recent trend. [427 C] (iii) The approach adopted by the Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem is not very commendable and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this court in appeal, was erroneous on the whole unsound. If this Court had erred in making those pronouncements it would be the first to admit such mistakes and to correct the error. After careful consideration of all the materials placed on record, we have found nothing to justify any doubt about the correctness of what was stated on the earlier occasion. [435 E G] (iv) The Tribunal was right in holding that questions which could justify a revision of the judicial opinion expressed on an experi mental occasion about a particular trend must be strong and unambiguous. The Court did not notice any slowing down of this trend. That is why an award can be revised or altered to correct to correct it.

The first respondent was the Chairman of a company Law Board. The second respondent was appointed as an Inspector for investigating the affairs of the Barium Chemicals Ltd., appellant No. 1 before the Board. On June 4, 1965, the Company preferred a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the Punjab High Court for the issue of a writ of mandamus or other appropriate writ directing the company Law Boards and Inspectors from giving effect to the order dated May 19, 1965 and also sought some other incidental reliefs. The order was challenged on the ground that the Chairman had acted mala fide because no honest opinion was formed on the matters which under the section give rise to the power but on irrelevant and extraneous material and further because the order was passed under the influence and malice of a Minister of Cabinet who was interested in another Company belonging to his sons and sought this means to oust a rival. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there were circumstances suggesting that as stated in the order of May 19 the Board had acted on material extraneous to the matters mentioned in section 237(b) of the ; (1) that the provisions of section 237 (b) were void as offending articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of ' the Constitution; (2) that there was ample material before the board on which it could and did form the opinion that there had been circumstances suggesting the need for action under section 237. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the power conferred on the Central Government by section 237 of the , to order an investigation and delegated by it to the company law Board is administrative that it can be validly exercised by the Chairman by an order made in pursuance of a rule enacted by the Central Govern ment under section 642(1) read with section 10E (5), that the exercise of the power does not violate any fundamental right of the company, that there the opinion to be formed under section 236 is subjective and that if the grounds are disclosed by the Board the Court can examine them for considering whether they are relevant. The power conferred by section 239(b)(a) is merely administrative it is difficult to appreciate how the allocation of business of the Board relating to the exercise Of such power can be anything other than a matter of procedure. For sub section (6) of section 10 E, I am inclined to construe this rule making power liberally and the Central Govt has power to constitute the company 's board to control (1)(2) 342 The power is conferred on it but under the Companies Act, 1951, a Board of Company Law Administration consisting of a Chairman and a member has been set up.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to five years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . The High Court, on appeal by special leave, held that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, and therefore it was necessary always to start with the lesser presumption and draw the higher presumption only when there is some other evidence to show the complicity of the persons in the crime itself. In appeal by Special Leave, HELD : The law advocated by Mr. Chari is not correct. If there is other evidence, to connect an accused with the crime, it may be drawn. It is not necessary to state categorically in this case that the person with whom the goods were found were the dacoits themselves. This presumption has been drawn and in our opinion rightly in this ease. [723 A] In the present case, the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market. These goods were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen.) A large number of persons said to be 20 in number pelted stones at the cart men and looted the property. Immediately afterwards a number of searches were made and the goods found with various persons who were prosecuted as offenders and they had been presumed to be involved in the dacoity itself. It may be 723 impossible to think that these 20 persons were merely receivers of stolen property from some other 20 persons who are the dacoits. The time gap in some cases is as short as two days and in some others it is not more than five days. In two cases only the time gap is about 19 days. Even then, the time lag is too short for original offenders to have disposed of the property to these appellants Or to have left the goods in their custody till such time as the original offenders could take them away.

In Miscellaneous Writ Petition, the petitioners have challenged the provisions of section 5 of the (12 of 1919) (hereinafter called 'the Act). It was contended that though the Act is a Central enactment it is possible of unjust and unjustified discriminatory im plation as it is left to each State Government to determine what substance they would include as poison and regulated, and the decision in one State to include the substance as poison is not automatically made applicable to the other States. The object of the enactment was to regulate the posses sion for sale and sale of the same. In exercise of this power by the Notification No. F 10/44/72 fin. (G) dated 7.8.1973, the Lt. Governor amended the Delhi Poisons Rules, 1926 as a result thereof, amending the Delhi Subordinate Rules, by including to the list of substances included in the Rules as "Poisons" "the substance commonly known as 'thinner ' containing spirit and other soluble material such as shellac in which the percentage of such solu ble material did not exceed 30% as poison. The petitioners contended that although the Act was a Central Act it is ordinarily possible of harsh and unjustified discrimina tion as it was left to every State Government, to specify what substance them would include. It was further submitted that the restrictions imposed on possession for sale was not reasonable restrictions. The respondents contend ing in their counter statement that the Act as well as the 1982 Act were regulatory the petitioners contended before the authorities that in substance manufactured by them did not come within Rule 2(x)(2) and there were some correspondence in this regard, when the competent authority held that the substance manufactured was manufacturing only those thinners which contain only liquid substances like as ecotone, ethyl acetate SDS etc. and was not all solubles. The respondent contended that in essence manufactured by the petitioners did not came within Rule II(2). Allowing the writ petition this Court HELD: 1.1 The provisions of neither section 2 nor 5 nor the impugned notification are hit by any consti tutional limitation. [227H] 1.2 The provisions in both the Acts which show that a substance known as "thinerner" as it taken is or mixing with some other substances are taken as intoxicating spirit endangering the life. [229B C] 2.3 Section 4 of the Act expressly sets out certain guidelines when the State can notify a substance as confession. It states that the State Government may by rule regulate the possession of any specified poison in any local area in which it the use of such poison for the purpose of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle appears to it be of such frequent occurrence as to render restriction on the possis tion thereof desirable. Any substance which is used for purposes mentioned therein can definitely be declared as poison for tho entire country. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance, as poisoning on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that area and the need to regu late the possession and sale in that areas. No question of discrimination can arise in such circumstances.

The appellant firm carried on business in drugs, chemicals, mercury camphor and art silk yam and as many as seven partners were admitted to the benefits of the partnership. The firm had dealings for several years with a firm known as "Bhojaji Sobhachand", carrying on business at Bombay as importers of yam & also as agents and adathias. The appellant firm was given dividends, but in appeal the amount was allowed in the return of income for the assessment year 1952 53 which included interest of Rs. 2,68,385 written off as irrecoverable. The Income tax Appellate Tribunal confirmed this order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the loans made by the assessee were not loan '; and (2) the debt or any part thereof was in respect of loans in the ordinary course of money lending business, but a debt representing loss sustained in the other business. HELD: The question should have been referred to the High Court for its opinion. [422 D] (a) (b). It gives no reasons in support of the conclusions reached by the Tribunal that the sum in question was not one incurred in the course of the assessee 's business as Chemists and Druggists nor in respect thereof. [420 A C] (c) The Tribunal has found that the monies sent by the appellant to the Bombay firm were never loans made in the normal course of its money lending trade, nor in any respect of any other business of the asses see. This finding covers the entire amount sought to be deducted and there is a flow of moneys to the Madras firm up to October 31, 1952 when the last of remittances was sent to it before the firm collapsed in about April 1952. [414 D E] (d) The tribunal has found in the documents produced by the Department that the sums in question were not loans made to the assessee. These findings are supported by the evidence on record.

The petitioners were the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of Sections 17 and 19 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. Under the provisions Of Section 36 of the Act, where the acquisitions, otherwise than by agreement, it will be regulated by the provisions as far they are applicable, of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (the Land Acquisition 'Act). The petitioners contended that as the awards in these cases had not been made within two years of the notification making the declaration under Section 4 of the 1894 Act, the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed. That contention was repelled along with certain other contentions in the judgment of the High Court which is sought to be impugned before this Court. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with frank and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so and suppresses material facts, his application is liable to be dismissed. [566C] 2. In the instant case, the Special leave petitions are liable to have been rejected. [666D] 3. The petitioners had obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in question in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the order of the Karnataka High Court dated August 14, 1984, with which we are not directly concerned here. The said interim orders have a direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts.

(2) In cl. 5 the adjustment was made in accordance with cl. 6 which provided for actual calculations starts with the words "subject to rules (i), (ii)" and therefore, the actual calculation made under cl.(iv) must be subject to clauses (a), (b) and (c) of el. (iv). [904 D E] Prakashchand Mehra vs Union of India, ; and Prakash Chand Mehta vs The Bank of workmen, ; followed.
