I.O. 47 of 1976, uses the words "within the meaning o sub section" of section " have to be given full meaning; in other words, the exemption under section 10 has to be restricted only to export sales falling outside the scope Of section 5. Clause 9 (21)(a) refers to cases where raw materials are purchased and exported and the word 'export ' was defined in section 2(e) as meaning "the taking out of the goods from the 361 State to any place outside it otherwise than by way of sale in tho course of inter state trade or commerce.

The appellants were registered dealers under the Bombay Sales Tax Act. The goods were sold by the sellers to the buyers on shipment basis. The sellers ' case was that these sales were made on FOB contracts and therefore they entered the export stream, and so no tax was realisable on these sales in view of the provisions of article 286(1)(b). Held, that the words " a person " in section 10(b) mean a registered dealer to whom he has sold the goods. If such despatch outside the State of Bombay is by a person to whom the certifying dealer has sold goods but who is not a registereddealer for despatch of the goods outside the state of Bombay, the purchasing dealer may not be liable for having made a false declaration ". The scheme of the Legislature clearly was that where the intention as declared had not been carried out purchase tax should be levied. In the present case the intention of the parties was that in compliance with the requirements of cl. 5(2) of the Exports (Control) Order, 1954, the goods shall be the property of the licensee at the time of export would therefore mean nothing more than that the property in the goods should pass immediately before the ship goes beyond the territorial waters of the country or at the earliest when the ship leaves the port. Whichever view is taken there was nothing to indicate that the intention to comply with the requirement of el.

The respondent husband married the appellant wife as a second wife, way back in 1956 and a few years later had a son by her. The initial warmth vanished and the jealousies of a triangular situation erupted, marring mutual affection. The respondent divorced the appellant around July 1962. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. For instance it recited that this respondent had transferred the suit premises, namely, a flat, in Bombay, to the appellant and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. There was a clause in the compromise that the appellant declares that she has now no claim or right whatsoever against the defendant or against the estate and the properties of the defendant. The appellant finding herself in financial straits and unable to maintain herself, moved the magistrate under section 125 Cr. P.C., 1973 for a monthly allowance for the maintenance of herself and her child. She proceeded on the footing that she was still a wife while the respondent rejected this status and asserted that she had been a divorcee. The Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that the respondent was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for her subsistence taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay where the parties lived, was high, and that the Respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appel lant. This order was challenged before the Sessions Judge by the aggrieved husband who on a strange view of the law that the court under section 127 had no jurisdic tion to consider whether the applicant was a wife, dismissed the petition in allowance of the appeal. The High Court rejected the revision petition and summarily dismissed a revision petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the courts below had surprisingly forgotten the plain provision in the Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code which provides that "wife ' includes a woman who has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from her husband and has not remarried. On behalf of the respondent it was urged that the Courts below had strangely forgotten that the plain provisions in the explanation (b), set up anywhere in the courts, below or urged before them. The contention was apparently based upon contractual arrangement in the consent decree read with section 127(3) (b). Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The scheme of the complex of provi sions in Chapter IX has a social purpose. Ill used wives and desparate divorcees shall not be driven to material and moral dereliction to seek sanctuary in the streets. This traumatic horror animates the amplitude of section 127 (3) is dynamic and its meaning cannot he pedantic but purposeful. The proposition, therefore, is that no husband can claim under section 126(3)(b) absolution from this obligation under section125 towards a divorced wife except on proof of payment of a sum stipulated by customary or personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance. [78C E] 1.2. The compulsive conclusion from a divorce by a husband and his provision of a separate residence as evidenced by the consent decrees fills the bill. Do divorcees have to 1) prove mutual consent to live apart; Divorce painfully implies that the husband orders her out of the conjugal home. If law has nexus with life this argument is still born. The last defence, based on meharhar payment merits more serious attention. The contractual limb of the contention must easily fail. [79D E] 2.1 In the normal course, an order for maintenance must follow, the quantum having been determined by the learned Magistrate at the trial level.

An order of the Collector was challenged by a person who had secured higher marks in a public auction and the matter was referred to the Collector under section 35 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1955. The Collector dismissed the petition holding that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. Aggrieved, the appellant filed an appeal before the Collector contending inter alia that there is no requirement specified in the Rule and the respondent was right. The Tribunal set aside the order and directed that the appellant be placed in the black list in respect of future contracts under the Collector is set aside. In this appeal on behalf of the State it was submitted that there has been no requirement and there is a clear clause in the Rules that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural justice. Dismissing the Appeal, HELD: 1.1 The last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing of the appellant in respect future contracts, cannot be sustained in law. [867A B] 1.2 An implied principle of the rule is of the law that any person affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. In that view of the matter, the last portion is setaside. [869C D] PG NO 869 PG NO 837 PG NO 860 2.3 The last paragraph in so insofar as it directed black listing cannot be held to be a elementary principle of natural Justice that parties affected by an order should not have right to open and making representation against the orders.

The property which was the subject matter of the dispute originally formed part of an extent of land situat ed on Mount Road, Madras bearing door Nos. 2 and 3 and a building thereon. The rent for the premises was Rs. 150 p.m. fixed under the lease deed. On 30.7.1953 all the co owners of the property (includ ing G.G.) sold the property to the United India Life Assur ance Company and the New Guardian of India Life Insurance Company Ltd. In 1956, the Life Insurance Corporation of India stepped into the shoes of these two insurance companies and became the owner of the said property. On 20.7 .65, the LIC moved two applications (being HRC Nos. 3310 and 3311) in the court of the Rent Controller (Sri A. Varadarajan who later became a Judge of the Supreme Court) for fixation of fair rent in respect of the premises covered by exhibit P 1. The fair rent claimed was computed at Rs.2,399.03 per month in respect thereof against the rent of Rs.150 p. m. fixed by the lease deeds. So far as item 2 was concerned it appears that at the time of hearing it was conceded before the Rent controller that the respondents were tenants of the entire properties covered by the said lease deed and that they had not constructed any of the structures thereupon. The Court, on a perusal of the sale deed dated 30.07.53 filed by the LIC before it came to the conclusion that the buildings on the land leased under exhibit P1 had also been conveyed to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation offair rent in regard thereof and that, therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the Rent Control Controller 's order in respect whereof the premises were only a vacant piece of land. The Rent Controller held that the building on the said land had also not been conveyed by the Life Assar ance company and that it was entitled tO fix the fair rent accordingly. The petitioner, who had retired as a respondent before the High Court, was given notice to submit his objections in respect of the preliminary list. The petitioner filed an affidavit and showed that the provisional gradation list was provisional. However, the legal position obtaining on such provisional seniority list was not prepared after hearing objections. The High Court held that the case now before this court is also governed by what was held by this Court in Shankariah 's case with reference to an entirely different and provisional list of Forest Officers. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and order of the Mysore High Court dismissing it was, HELD: 1.1 The combined final gradation list dated April 6, 1962 so far as category 6 is concerned is ultra vires and illegal and that part of the notification alone must be quashed by grant of a writ in the nature of certiorari. [ 828B C] Shankari vs Ram Chand & Ant. ; , 224; Shri Bhagwan & Anr. vs Ramchand & Ant., ; , 222, referred to. 1.2 The combined provisional gradation List dated April 4, 1962 is ultra vided and illegal. [827F G] 1.3 In the instant case since no such opportunity was furnished to the respondents with regard to those two matters, they were bound by the provisions of the Act. [829G] Shankhadkar & Ors. vs R.D. Nanjiah; , ; 2.1 In view of the special circumstances of the present case, this Court is of the view that a Court cannot go into the merits or otherwise of equation of posts which is a matter within the province of the Central Government. [828C] 1:2 The respondents were entitled to an opportunity to make a representation with regard t he two points urged by the petitioner before the final gradation lists, being published and published as a final list. A right to represent was recognised as existing at time when the list was still to be considered as not finalised presumably because some mistakes had crept in due to want of heating on two points. Clearly what was meant was that the publication gave the list finality. In that particular case, the fist had been prepared without due regard to the particular important point which had to he considered before finalisation. What has observed does not mean that if a final List is prepared contrary to the rules applicable or is vitiated on some ground showing that a condition precedent to the finalisation of the list is absent, it would still be inviolable ,Dr sacrosanct.

The petitioners in both these writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of polished diamonds. The Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March, 1991 in para 174 of the Import & Exports Policy for April 1988 to March 1979 in para 215 made provision for grant of certain import facilities to Export Houses which were registered in accordance with the provisions of the said Policy. One of the conditions was that the Export House would be eligible to Additional Licences on the basis of the export actually made in preceding three licensing years termed as 'the Base period '. The petitioners submitted application for registration as Export Houses and for grant or renewal of Export House Certificate which would have entitled them to the grant of such Additional Licence. The said applications were rejected by the authorities on the view that they had failed to diversify their export of "Other products" during the year 1977 78. The order refusing the Export Certificate was challenged by the petitioners by filing writ petitions under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Bombay High Court which dismissed the same. While the said appeal and other writ petition (filed by the Petitioners viz. Writ Petition No. 460 of 1988) were pending in the Bombay, this Court decided Civil Appeal No. 1423 of 1984, Union of India vs Rajnikant Brothers, and other connected matters by order dated April 18, 1985 wherein it was observed that there was no requirement of diversification of exports as a condition for grant/ entitlement of Export Houses in the Import Policy for 1978 79 and the Export Houses who were issued Additional Licences prior to April 1, 1988, on the ground that they have failed to carry out their export obligations during the period 1977 78 in accordance therewith. The Court further directed the authorities to grant Export House Certificates to the petitioners under the Import and Export Policy 1978 79 within three months. While construing the aforesaid direction contained in its order dated 4th April, 1985 in Rajnarayanikant Brothers case (supra) this Court has held that the grantees of the Additional Licences were not only prohibited from importing items which were excluded under the Export Policy1978 79 but also from importing item excluded under Import Policy prevailing at the time of import and that the word 'banned ' was intended to take in terms which were banned altogether as well as items which are `non canalised ' and also item which are 'canalised ' could not be ruled out and it was in this light that the Court can be said to have used the words "whether canalised or otherwise ' contained in the order dated 1st April, 1988. The High Court further held that under Import & export Policy 197879 Additional licences were to be given on the basic basis of one third of the f.o.b. value of the exports made in 1977 78 whereas under Import and export policy 1988 91 Additional Licences are to be granted on the same basis as permissible during the licensing year to which the application pertains, but the items to be allowed will be as per the Import policy in force on the date of issue of the licence. The grievance of the petitioners is confined to sub para (10) of para 218 which lays down that Additional licences issued to Export House/Trading Houses prior to 1st March, 1988 shall cease to be valid for import of items of raw materials, components and consumables covered by Appendices 3 and 5 Part A and items of non OGL capital goods (other than those covered by Appendix 1 Part A) and items available under this Policy.

The appellant is a division of McDowell & Co. Ltd., which manufactures and sells fusel oil/Styrene Monomer falling under Tariff Item No. 68 of the Ist Schedule to the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944. The case of the appellant is that the said fusel Oil is a com pletely manufactured article and after completion of its manufacture it is stored in storage tanks duly approved for this purpose. It is also the case of appellant that the manufacture of fusel gas is complete and it is the fully manufactured fusel oils/Stirene Mendenceer Monomers falling under tariff Item No 68 of Ist Schedule of the Act. The appellant had filed its price lists in respect of the same. In the said price lists, which were duly approved by the Asstt. Collector, the appellant had shown the value of furosel oil at the rate of Rs. 10,000/ . In the price lists which were initially approved by Asstt. Collec tor, the assessee had shown its value of Crylic acid and also the value at which those were sold in wholesale as "naked Ex Works" and in bulk. The said price list was duly approved and the appellant filed its prices lists in regard to the same, but the Department did not include the cost of packing in the assessable value. The Tribunal held that at the time of removal, the goods were delivered from the factory in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer, there fore, the value had to be included in the deter mination value. Hence according to the appellant it is not necessary for the said Cryodicon to be supplied to the customers in drums in the aforesaid situation. The question whether the cost oat of the drums supplied by the customer for which he is not charged should be included In the assessable Value or not would depend upon whether the goods in question are supplied in a packed condition or not. If the manufacturer supplies the drums and charges the customers separately, then under section 4(4)(d)(i), the cost price of such packing would have to be added to the price except where the packing is of durable nature and returnable to the manufacturer. The proper interpretation to be placed on the words of section 4 (4)(D)(i) has been explained in the judgment of this Court in Union of India & Ors. vs Bombay Tyre International Ltd., ; and held that the "value" of the excisable article has to be computed with reference to the value charged by the manufacturer, the computation being made in accordance with the terms of section4. It has also to be borne in mind that in any event in so far as Styrene Moulder Oil is concerned, the price of the drum in which it is packed is not includible in the assess able value of the goods.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Head Clerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. PW 3, the Principal of the training School issued exhibit P 2 show cause notice to the PW 1, Venkataswamy, the canteen contractor as to why his licence for running the canteen should not be cancelled. This was on the basis of a complaint made by the appellant that the food served in the canteen was substand ard. The appellant produced the currency notes. PW 6 conducted the phenolphthalein test with reference to the fingers of the appellant. The test was positive, the currency note were seized and the appellant arrested. At the trial, the prosecution witnesses supported the case. PW 1 affirmed the fact that the appellant made the demand and had also received the amount on 22.10 .1975 itself passed orders and closed the file. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence, rejected the plea of the appel lant and recorded the conviction. Before this Court it was contended for the appellant: (i) that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the accused had not been examined; (ii) that the conviction under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section161 I. P.C.; (iii) that even though the conviction was under section 165 I.I.P., and section5(2), of the Act is not attracted on the proved facts is also not impressive; and (iv) that it was highly improbable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution has failed to prove the guilt of the appellants in view of the presumption arising under section 4(1) of Prevention of Corrup tion Act which has not been rebutted. [337F] 2. The conviction cannot therefore be sustained. [340C] 3. The burden resting on the accused person in such a case would not be as light as it is where a presumption is raised under section 114 of Evidence Act and cannot be held to be discharged merely by reason of the fact of that the explanation offered by the accused is reasonable and probable. It must further be shown that the Explanation is a true one. The words 'unless the contrary is proved ' which occur in this provision make it clear that the presumption has to be rebutted by 'proof ' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, there fore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to ' be rebutted. On a careful consideration of the facts and circum stances, this court is not satisfied that the appe lant had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption. [341E F] 4.

It is evident from the phraseology used in cl.(a) i. e. property wrongfully obtained and (b) of sub section 1, for the contentions that cl.(a) and therefore both clauses (a), and (c) must be read together. In essence, the submission is that sub section provides for the launching of a prosecution against an officer or employees of a Company for wrongful possession of such properties under cls. The appellant was the founder of a private temple. The deity installed in the temple was intended by the Founder to be continually worshipped by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindu public and not merely on that basis the grant was continued by the Government. The appellant contended that the Sansthan was a private property and it was also transferred to the Shishya Adhikari to maintain it as his own property. Held, that the temple is a public trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. The expression in the recital that "you are free as the full owner thereof" does not convert the gift which is expressly in favour of the deity or Sansthan into that in favour by an individual as private property. The object and purpose for which the trust was created, the consistent manner in which the property has been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner in Which the property had long been used by the public, the contribution of the public to all intents and purposes, as a matter of right without the least interference or restriction from the temple authorities, to foster maintenance of the worship of the accretion to the trust property by way of grants from the state of gifts from outsiders inconsistent with the private nature of the trust, the nature of devolution of the property, are all important elements in determination of the question whether a property is a private or a public religious endowment. The word "buwa" means a place by whatever designation known and used as a place of public religious worship and dedicated to or for the benefit of or used as of right by the Hindu community or any section thereof as a Place of public Religious worship. The definition in the deed of nomination that the property is the private property, does not alter its character merely because ownership of the donor is transferred to it. It is only when the beneficiaries are not members of a family or a specified individual, then the endowment can only be regarded as public intended to benefit the general body of worshippers.

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 1948 and 1951 52 by the Third Income tax Officer, C. 1 Ward Bombay, at and for Rs. 40,178 4 0. The assessee not having paid up the assessed amount of tax the Income tax officer on the 10th April 1951 issued a warrant of arrest under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 requiring the assessee to appear before him in person on the 16th June 1955 and show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in satisfaction of the said certified demand. The sale proclamation was held on the 25th February 1955 fetching a price of Rs. 33,000 and it was confirmed on the 30th March 1955. The sales proclamation was issued on the 15th January 1955. On the 16st June 1955 an application was made by the present petitioner to the Bombay High Court under article 226 for quashing the said order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 offends article 14 of the Constitution and that article 21 and article 14 were not void under article 13(1). On appeal by special leave: Held, that the law impugned before this Court has only adopted for its own purpose, the same coercive process which was devised by the States for their own purposes which are closely akin or similar to the purpose of the Union. The law was not dead and could not be assailed as repugnant to article 14 Of the Constitution. It was not correct to say that all the provisions of all the State laws for recovery of arrears of land revenue had been referentially incorporated in section 46 (2) at the time it was enacted to be treated as crystallised and to be applied by the Collectors, although the State law laws for the recovery of dues of land Revenue may be materially altered by sub sequent amendment. The classification has been made Statewise and it is clear that in the matter of payment of public demands of the States the people of different States are not similarly situated and their own States have imposed on them such coercive processes as the circumstances and needs of each State require. The laws impugned before us had only adopted, for its proper purpose, it was a plausible argument to say, that all provisions of the State Laws for recovery Of arrears of Land Revenue had been referredentially incorporated into section 46.(2) so as to provide for the detention of all defaulters for the same period in all cases in all States. The discrimination complained of is not unconstitutional for the simple reason that the impugned law was based on a territorial classification having a reasonable nexus or correlation between that basis of classification and the object sought to be achieved by the Act. In the present case the classification has, therefore, been made by Statewise, and it cannot be assailed in view of the provisions contained in section 13 as it originally stood and not by it as subsequently amended. The position was different even though the State legislatures have imposed upon them such drastic processes as recovery of land tax demand.

The appellants are the trustees of a Port Trust Employees ' Union. The respondents to this appeal are the Trustees of the Port of Bombay. The dispute in the present case is whether the existing system of work of shore crew of the Prince 's and Victoria Docks under which each shift was broken up into 8 hours ' duty, 2 hours ' variable recess and 12 hours ' overtime needs any modification? The Tribunal held that the Union was not able to establish that the existing practice of work needed any modification. The appellants contended that the break up of a 12 hours shift into 8 days ' work, 2 hour ' rest and 2 hours respectively did not violate the provisions of the , and that the so called period of rest was illusory since being variable, it was some times given right at the commencement of the shift and some times at the end depending on the tides or the exigencies of the work. The Union contended that a 12 hour ' shift should be divided into 8 minutes ' work and 4 hours ' and overtime as was the case with the Flotilla Crew. They also contended that in any case the period of 9 hours must always include intervals of rest, and spread over of the working time. Held: (i) The provisions of section 13(2)(c) read with section 13 (3) give us an indication of what is meant by an interval of rest; (ii) The scheme of the compels the inclusion of an hour of rest in a normal working day because the total number of work hours in a six day week cannot go beyond 48. (iii) The workmen compared the case of the Master 's & Victoria Dock with the cases of the Alexandra Docks and the FlytillaCrew or the crew at the Alexantra Dock.

The disputed property was let out on June 25, 1976. The accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika Ghaziabad with effect from October 1, 1976 and the suit was filed for eviction after termination of tenancy before the trial court and objection was raised that as the shop and the basement were separately let out the tenancy could not be terminated by a single notice that would be invalid. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court set aside this conclusion of the trial Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that apart from the controversy about the date which should be the starting point for computing the period of 10 years in view of the language of Sections 39 and 40 of the Act, provisions of this Act will be applicable to the present case and therefore a decree for eviction could only be passed. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that as during the pendency of the proceedings in this Court 10 years have elapsed even if the date of completion is taken to be 1.10.76 which is the date on which the first assessment of this property was made and during the course of this matter 1.11.76 had been crossed now the period for exemption has come to an end and therefore the appellant tenant will be entitled to the benefit of the provisions of Section 20. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The right of the parties will be determined on the basis of the rights available to them on the date when the suit is filed and not subsequently. [164D] 1.2 In order to attract section 39 the suit must be pending on the day of commencement of this act i.e. 15.7.1972 and therefore it could not he contended that the present revision petition or the appeal either to the High Court or the appellate authority arose out of suit which was pending on that date. [165E F] 1:3 The restriction put under Section 20 is to the institution of the suit itself and therefore, it is clear that during the proceedings 10 years had elapsed even though the period has expired, the restriction will not be attracted as the suit has been instituted within 10 years and therefore restriction as provided for in Section 20 can not be applicable. [166G] 1 :4 The restriction placed under Section 2(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 is to that institution itself and it is true that the language used by the section is not identical with the language in Section 39 and is a decision of a Bench of three Judges which is binding on this Court.

The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment of three persons, namely Abdul Rahim, Abdul Hamid and Abdul Gaffur from the property in suit (a parcel of land about 1 cottah 8 chittaks being part of premises No. 6 /1 Shibtola Lane), Calcutta. In the notice to quit served on the 7th May 1948, the first two defendants were described as thika tenants under the plaintiff and the third as a person who had purported to purchase the structures on the land and the tenancy right therein. The suit was contested only by the third defendant who filed a written statement in September 1948 contending that the suit was bad for non joinder of parties. The trial court decreed the suit but the appellate Court held that at the time when the appeal of the respondent was disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, the rights of the parties were governed by the Thika Tenancy Act of 1949 and the definition of thika tenant in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. On a further appeal by the second defendant, the High Court held (i) that the appellant was not liable to ejectment in the absence of any grounds therefor in the notice dated June 18, 1948, as he was a thikatenant within the meaning of the Act as it was finally amended; and (ii) that even if no proceedings were pending in any court, it was open to the landlord to file a suit. In appeal by certificate to this Court, HELD: The benefit of section 28 was available only if the decree or order for recovery of possession had been made before the date of commencement of the 1949 Act but possession of such holding had not been recovered from him. If any pending suit or proceeding related to any matter in respect of which the Controller was competent to pass orders, the suit or proceedings would be transferred to the controller who would deal with it in accordance with the provisions of the West Bengal Thika Thika Amendment Ordinance 1952, i.e., 21st October 1952 and not in February 1949 i. e. the date when the commencement of that Act, it is not open to a landlord either to allege any of the grounds specified in section 3 or to prove the existence thereof at the hearing of the suit, he had to establish the existence of such a ground when the suit is heard. All that the section lays down is that ejectment could not be had unless the existence was one of the reasons was proved. [176 B C] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , followed. Mahadeodolal Jodia vs administrator General ofWest Bengal, , approved.

Prior to 1965, in the High Court of Allahabad Bench Secretaries were on a higher pay scale than that of Section Officers. They were in the pay scale of Rs. 160 320 as against the pay scales of Rs 120 300 to Section Officers, and there was no valid reason for giving them pay scale equal to Section officers or Private Secretaries. The Committee recommended for them a pay scale slightly lower than that given by the Pay Commission to Superintendents or the Section Officers and that they should also be given the same pay scale which is being given to Superintendents i.e. It was found that the nature of duties and responsibilities and the fact that every Honble Judge will have one Private Secretary in the scale of pay Rs.500 1,000 would raise a dispute as to the pay pay scale payable to Benches Grade I Officers with effect from October 1, 1975. The High Court referred the matter to an Arbitrator who submitted his report, but did not accept the claim of Bench Secretaries for giving him pay scale equivalent to Section Officer or Private Secretary. The Chairman of the Judicial Committee after considering the relevant factors recommended a pay of Rs 400 750 for Bench Secretaries and Rs. 500 1,00,000 to Section officer in its meeting held on February 1, 1973. The Secretary made an order dated July 2, 1976 providing that all Benches Union Territories would have one private Secretary in addition to be given their pay scale admissible to Section Assistant Secretaries with effectfrom October 1. 1975. On the basis of this order, the Pay Revision Committee recommended that the number of the posts of Bench Secretary be upgraded and placed in the Pay Scale of Rs,500 1000. The State Government accepted the recommendations. Subsequently, these pay scales were raised to Rs.200 450 and Rs 15 715 respectively. Being dissatisfied with the down grading, the Bench Secretaries made representation to the Government which was rejected. The appellants thereupon filed a writ petition before the High court. In the meantime, the pay of Bench Judges was revised to Rs, 2000 450 and a Group II PG NO 307 206 salaries were paid more emoluments than Section Officers because they were appointed through a competitive examination and they would not get the same salary and conditions of service as laid down under the Rules framed by the Chief Justice for the purpose of promotion to Bench Secretary Grade I. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. On behalf of appellants, it was contended: (i) When Judges in the subordinate judiciary are appointed on a different time scale of duties, they must receive the same wages and conditions as class IV employees; and (ii) the source from which theamanages were fixed is such that there can be and there are different grades in a service, with varying qualification for entry into a particular grade. (iii) The nature of work performed by persons of longer experience is superior than the work of newcomers. HELD: 1.1 On one time, Bench Secretaries Grade I are in the higher pay scales than Bench Secretaries grade II.

Respondent 1, the Special Area Development Authority for Korba Special Area, is constituted under section 65 of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam (23 of 1973). The Act was passed by the Madhya Pra desh Adhiniyam, 1973. Section 69(d) confers upon the Development Authority powers for the purpose of municipal administration and for the purposes connected with the matters aforesaid. Chapter VIII of the Act consisting of sections 64 to 71 is entitled "Special Areas". Section 64 empowers the State Government to declare any area as a special area by issuing a notification. Section 55 provides that for every Special Area there shall be a Special Area development Authority consisting of a Chairman and such other members as the Government may determine from time to time. Section 68 confers upon Development Authority power for the pur poses of municipal adminis trative administration and section 133 of the Municipal Corporation Act. The procedure for imposition of taxes is contained in section 129 of the Municipalities Act and section 135 of the said Act. By a notification dated March 15, 1977, published in Government Gazette, dated July 15,1977, the Development Author ity, Korba was directed under the aforesaid clauses of sections 68 and 69 to exercise the powers and perform the functions of a Class I Municipality constituted under the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act, 1961. The appellant Company challenged its liability to pay the property tax on the grounds, inter alia, that no tax was leviable on its property since the company was owned wholly by the Govern ment of India and that respondent 1 was estopped from levying the property Tax by reason of the agreement of 1976. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant Company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the provisions conferring powers of taxation under the two Acts must be taken to have been incorporated in section 69(D) of the M.P. Municipalities Act 1956, and any subsequent change in those provisions by amendment of the two statutes cannot be availed of by respondent 1; (ii) assuming that section 127A of the Municipality Act or section 135 thereof which were introduced by an amendment made after the enactment of section 69 (d), could be invoked for levying the Property tax, respondent 1 cannot impose that tax without following the procedure prescribed by sections 129 and 133 of Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act; and (iii) assuming section 127 A of the municipality Act or Section 135 of Municipal CorporationAct which were inserted by an amending Act made after enactment of s 69(c), could he invoked for levy the property taxes, respondent I cannot impose a tax without complying with the procedure laid down in sections 129 & 133 of M. P. Municipalities (Amendment) Act, 1976. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred by the State Legislature on Special Area Depart ment Authority to impose the propertytax on lands and buildings is therefore not in conflict with the power conferred under section 69 of the . [16C] 2.1 The power of taxation provided for in section 68(d), is subject to the overriding power of Parliament as declared in section 15 of the , which provides that nothing contained in Section 133 shall apply to the tax mentioned in clause (a) of sub section (1) of section 132, which shall be charged and levied in accordance with section 135. The three Acts are therefore supplemental from which it must follow that amendments made to the earlier Acts after the Act of 1973 did not result in invalidation of every State legislation relating to mines and minerals is demonstrated effectively by the decision in State of Haryana & Anr. vs Ishwari Khetan Sugar Mills (P) Ltd. vs The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 891, relied on.

The appellant was the lessee of a slate quarries in his estate for five years in succession commencing from February 1942, if the Rajah was satisfied with the work carried on by him during the preceding year. The lease was for 20 years commencing from the termination of the fifth year, but the lease was extended to 20 years. On December 10, 1947, the appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease granted by the Raja to him. No notice was issued to him as to why the lease should not be terminated without any compensation under the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The Board of Revenue refused to ratify the lease and terminated it under the powers delegated to it under r. 476 of 1957. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court praying for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the Madras State to forbear from terminating his leasehold right in the slate quarry quarries and from interfering with his possession and working of the slated quarries and other ancillary reliefs. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the lease had been granted prior or subsequent to July 1, 1945, and as the lease did not give three months ' notice to the appellant or provide for any compensation as required by section 20 of the Act, it was not enforceable against the Government according to the second Proviso to section20(1). The appellant came up in appeal to this Court. Held: (i) The rule only indicates the authority who is to decide whether the right falling under the first proviso should be terminated or allowed to continue. In other words, that rule does not attract the operation of the third proviso at all. Even if that rule has the effect contended for it cannot change the meaning of section 20 which we gather on a true construction thereof. (ii) The second proviso deals with the termination by the force of the second sub clause itself and (iii) rights created after July 1. 1945, if they are for a period exceeding one year, are liable to be avoided under the third sub clause.
